papers.title: Long-Context Generation Is a Sampling Problem (When You Turn Up the Heat)
papers.summary: The paper studies how the choice of sampler influences long‑context generation quality in open‑weight language models when the temperature is increased. By testing 29 models (1 B–122 B parameters) on ten benchmarks and a million‑token needle‑retrieval task, the authors compare samplers that keep a small, steady token pool to those that allow low‑probability tokens. They find that samplers such as top‑nsigma, which maintain a tiny pool, preserve accuracy even at temperature 2—keeping a median 100 % of their temperature‑1 score—while samplers like top‑p drop to 26 % and fail to solve many coding tasks, with a strong negative correlation (‑0.77) between pool size and judged quality.

papers.title: What MoE Routing Controls: Causal Interventions on Expert Trajectories
papers.summary: The paper studies how directing tokens along specific expert paths in a mixture‑of‑experts language model changes its behavior. By adding a fixed bias to the router logits for a chosen “target path” (either a format path that controls output style or a concept path that biases topic), the authors show that steering a format path can alter the text the model writes, while steering a concept path mainly shifts next‑token probabilities toward that concept but has little effect on the final output. They find that format paths reinforce themselves once started, that concepts such as religion and money have the strongest steering effect (especially in middle layers), and they analyze why the effect varies by looking at embedding distinctiveness and word frequency.

papers.title: Large Language Models as Nonlinear Dynamical Systems: The Three Clocks of Depth, Training, and Generation
papers.summary: The paper treats language models as nonlinear dynamical systems and builds a “Three‑Clock Dictionary” that maps fifteen nonlinear‑dynamics concepts onto the three clocks of depth, training, and generation, drawing on about 200 papers. It derives reduced‑order models for key components (softmax, gradient descent, loss spikes, attention, repetition loops) and tests them on open language models, finding that escape from repetition loops follows an Arrhenius law with a logit‑gap barrier that deepens then saturates, so the temperature needed to leave a loop falls like 1/ln N with generation length N and rises with model size. While the analysis shows coherent text lives in a narrow temperature window and that small transformers train at a multi‑mode edge of stability, the proposed escape‑analysis controllers remove loops but do not yet beat the best fixed temperature, and the authors outline twelve open problems for future work.

papers.title: Fine-Grained Japanese Clinical Named Entity Recognition: A Controlled Comparison of BERT and Open-Weight Large Language Models
papers.summary: The paper compares fine‑tuned BERT‑CRF baselines with nine open‑weight large language models on a Japanese clinical NER benchmark that defines 113 entity categories, using 433 test sentences and 1,672 training sentences. Models were evaluated in zero‑shot prompting (with or without JSON Schema constraints) and after QLoRA fine‑tuning, with output‑token limits of 900, 2,600, or 4,096 tokens, and performance was measured by relaxed and exact‑surface F1 scores. The results show that zero‑shot LLMs lag behind BERT (0.337 vs 0.836–0.841 relaxed F1), but fine‑tuned LLMs with at least 13B parameters and larger output limits surpass BERT (relaxed F1 0.882–0.914, exact‑surface 0.840–0.880), and increasing output limits improves recall and reduces length‑limited outputs, while JSON Schema constraints provide only marginal changes.

papers.title: What RL on Expert-Built Tasks Teaches Nemotron 3.5 Super
papers.summary: Researchers post‑trained NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3.5 Super (120 B total, 12 B active) with reinforcement learning on five expert‑built task datasets, training a fresh rank‑32 LoRA adapter with CISPO on Tinker for each dataset and comparing it directly to the base model. On twelve headline benchmarks the adapters improve performance by 4.5 to 13.8 points—IFBench +4.5, GDP_pdf +13.8, SWE‑bench Pro V2 +5.2, Terminal‑Bench 2.1 +6.4, MultiChallenge +8.3, AutomationBench +12.7, Chartography +11.2—and the document adapter alone adds 8.0 points on AutomationBench. The adapters also solve new tasks that the base model fails on, each addressing specific shortcomings such as tool‑use, coding, constraints, chart measurement, and spreadsheet reading.
